newsitem.title: FRANCE: Kohl says Buba gold could be used for E German debt.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says Buba gold could be used for E German debt.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Tuesday revaluation of the Bundesbank's gold reserves could be used to pay off debt inherited from former East Germany but would not be used towards the current federal budget.

Kohl, in Paris for talks with President Jacques Chirac on European Union integration, said the Bonn government and the German central bank had reached no agreement yet on the scale or on details of the controversial plan.
He reiterated Germany's insistence that there was no question of actually selling off gold.
"Upon reunification, the Federal Republic took on heavy debts which we have to bear," he told a news conference before a dinner with Chirac.
"If we reach a certain agreement (on gold revaluation) we would put the money into this (solidarity) fund to pay off these debts," Kohl said.
"Neither the scale nor the details have been decided," he said, adding it was "not the aim to bring the gold into the federal budget."

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said last week Germany would revalue Bundesbank gold and currency reserves to plug holes in the country's finances and improve its chances of qualifying for monetary union.

Those chances received a setback after an official estimate said 1997 tax revenues would be 18 billion marks ($10.6 billion) lower than previously forecast, casting doubt on whether Germany could meet tough deficit criteria for membership in the single currency.
Germany's announcement brought accusations from critics that it was resorting to "creative accounting" and undermining the country's hard earned credibility.
Revaluing Germany's near 3,000 tonne gold hoard would give its finances an on-paper windfall of around 40 billion marks, economists estimate.

The leaders' talks came three days before a special summit on EU reform and less than a week before the first round of a snap parliamentary election called by Chirac to clear the decks for France's participation in monetary union.
Chirac said France and Germany were in broad accord on EU reform issues and the two men had talked about preparations for the summit to be held on Friday in the Dutch town of Noordwijk.
"We reviewed virtually all of the issues" and the views of France and of Germany were "very broadly convergent," he said.
Chirac and Kohl also ruled out renegotiating the EU's "stability pact" meant to limit budget deficits under monetary union.
Asked at the news conference about a call by France's opposition Socialists for new talks on the pact, Kohl replied, "No. I don't see why."
Chirac said France had given its commitment and "nobody would accept or understand if we were to go back on our commitments."
EU leaders agreed on the stability pact last December in Dublin after months of wrangling between France and Germany over what form it should take.
